title: What Breaks When Packaging Moves From Wafer To Panel?
gist: Moving advanced packaging from 300mm wafers to panels offers large utilization gains (ASE shows 72 units on a 600mm panel versus 9 on a wafer for a 5.5x-reticle interposer), but exposes wafer-specific assumptions in coating, lithography, warpage, dicing and inspection. Yield and rework, not area, set the economic limit, and ASE's mixed flow splits a 600mm panel into four 300mm pieces before assembly.

insights.claim: A 5.5x-reticle interposer yields 9 units on a 300mm wafer versus 16 on a 300mm panel; a 600mm panel divided into four 300mm pieces yields 64 and the intact 600mm panel yields 72, so the intact panel produces 8 times the wafer's units despite only roughly five times the raw area.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Quantifies why panel-level packaging is compelling for large AI/HPC packages.
insights.locator: The economics behind that compromise are substantial.

insights.claim: Intel Foundry showed on a 510 x 515mm panel that a roughly 4x-reticle package yields about 10 units per 300mm wafer versus approximately 48 on the panel, and the largest square on a 300mm wafer is only about 210 x 210mm.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Wafer geometry is a hard limit for ever-larger AI packages, favoring panels.
insights.locator: The utilization advantage grows as the package does.

insights.claim: Intel's Tarek Ibrahim says wafers remain more economical for certain form factors, but beyond a certain size the panel becomes more effective, and AI's need for very large systems makes panels an obvious choice for scale.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Panel adoption is tied to package size growth driven by AI systems.
insights.quote: when you go beyond a certain form factor, you can see quickly that the panel becomes more effective
insights.locator: “For certain form factors, we believe a wafer is more economical,”

insights.claim: ASE's Teck Chong Lee says assembly on a 600mm panel is high risk because not all equipment exists, so ASE completes the interposer in large format then divides it into four pieces for assembly and C4, a lower-risk approach.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Mixed-format flows show equipment readiness, not geometry, limits panel adoption near term.
insights.quote: The risk of doing the assembly on the 600mm panel is high
insights.locator: “The risk of doing the assembly on the 600mm panel

insights.claim: Many assumptions that looked like process requirements were actually wafer requirements: spin coating relies on radial symmetry and gives uneven film at rectangular corners with most resist wasted, so 600mm panel flows use slit or slot-die coating over roughly 586 x 586mm active area, and maskless direct imaging displaces wafer steppers in many panel flows.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Panel transition creates opportunities for coating and direct-imaging equipment vendors over wafer-tool incumbents.
insights.locator: Part of the challenge is that familiar wafer processes

insights.claim: Wafer-level packaging is a single-sided process while panel is dual-sided, and managing uniformity and Cpk at panel scale is a challenge according to Intel's Ibrahim.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Process control complexity raises ramp risk for panel lines.
insights.quote: On panel, it’s actually a dual-sided process.
insights.locator: “At wafer level, it’s a single-sided process,”

insights.claim: As line and space moves from roughly 5um toward 2um and below, fine-line RDL on glass panels needs new photoresists, tighter overlay control and uniform temperature across large areas, but panels cannot inherit round-300mm front-end equipment or traditional substrate tools, leaving panel packaging between the two.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Equipment gap between front-end and substrate tooling is an opening for new panel-specific tool suppliers.
insights.locator: Those differences propagate into the materials

themes.theme: Yield and rework set the limit

insights.claim: Amkor's Mike Kelly says a tiny yield hit that loses super-expensive silicon can erase the benefits of larger scale, so repair and rework are required to avoid losing the whole benefit of getting large.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Yield on high-value logic-plus-HBM panels is the key variable for panel economics.
insights.quote: a tiny yield hit, and the loss of some of that super-expensive silicon, will just blow all the benefits
insights.locator: “There’s so much money in chips going onto a wafer or panel

insights.claim: A panel carrying logic and HBM can hold tens of thousands of dollars of known-good silicon before some package-level failures become visible, and keeping the 600mm panel intact gains an extra 12.5% usable area but moves into a format harder to control.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: The largest manufacturable panel may not be the most economical one.
insights.locator: That matters more as the value assembled

insights.claim: In RDL formation tests, average dimensional shift at three sigma was about 22 microns for standard high-Tg organic material, about 7 microns for ultra-low-CTE material and about 3 microns for glass core, according to Fraunhofer IZM, with glass possibly nearing the measurement accuracy limit.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Quantified dimensional-stability advantage supports glass substrate adoption.
insights.quote: The standard high-Tg material showed an average shift of about 22 microns at three sigma,

insights.claim: Brewer Science notes glass carriers are rigid, CTE-matchable and smooth for fine pitch, but non-linear die shift during thermal processing is hard to correct, especially on large glass panels.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Glass is not a free fix: die-shift correction remains an open issue.
insights.quote: non-linear die shift during thermal processing

insights.claim: Each process step leaves the panel slightly different for the next, so a die placed correctly early can end up elsewhere after curing or deposition, and the next layer must be built on the panel that exists, not original coordinates.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Feed-forward metrology and adaptive patterning become necessary at panel scale.
insights.locator: That turns process history into an alignment problem.

insights.claim: Simulation of warpage and stress is limited because newer glass and polymer systems lack mature temperature-dependent modulus data, and the best data may be proprietary; Synopsys advises simulating with generic properties before experiments.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Materials characterization data sharing is a bottleneck and opportunity for suppliers and simulation vendors.
insights.quote: Before you fail your manufacturing or your yield, do simulation. Don’t speculate,
insights.locator: “Before you fail your manufacturing or your yield

insights.claim: ASE's Lee says the 600mm panel layout must be designed from the start around separation into four 300mm panels, and cutting required several steps plus edge processing to remove sharp edges.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Dicing becomes an upstream design constraint, affecting layout and throughput.
insights.quote: You have to design the layout of the 600mm panel from the start
insights.locator: “You have to design the layout of the 600mm panel

insights.claim: Through-glass vias concentrate stress because copper expands faster than glass, producing compressive stress on heating and tensile stress on cooling that can drive circumferential cracks, and Applied Materials says there is no industry standardization for thermal testing to find them.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Glass-core reliability requires new metrology and standards, a gating item for adoption.
insights.quote: There is no standardization in the industry today,
insights.locator: “There is no standardization in the industry today,”

insights.claim: Critical Manufacturing's Tiago Tavares says recipes that work in demonstrations meet variation across lots and tools in mass production, and some needed controls must be invented.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Expect a learning curve and software/controls spend during panel ramp.
insights.quote: some of the controls you need to invent because they are not yet there

insights.claim: The article argues panel-level packaging may not converge on a single standard format as 300mm wafers did; a 600mm panel may suit coating and RDL while smaller formats suit assembly, so different flow stages may use different substrate formats.
insights.speaker: Gregory Haley
insights.so_what: Equipment ecosystems may fragment across formats, complicating bets on a single panel standard.
insights.locator: ASE’s mixed-format approach suggests the transition may be less tidy.
